lesson.menu_title: Past Perfect for Turnaround Stories -- What Had Already Happened Before You Arrived
lesson.menu_desc: Tell a project story in two layers: the situation you inherited and what you did about it -- 32 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 11 -- Past Perfect for Turnaround Stories
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Lucia Nishiyama Serra | Lesson 11 -- Past Perfect for Turnaround Stories

listenings.text: Hi, this is the post-incident summary for last Thursday, recorded before the written report goes out. Here is what we know. The service went down at six forty in the morning. By the time the on-call engineer opened the dashboard, the queue had already grown to four hundred thousand messages, and two regions had failed over. The team restored service in fifty minutes, and that part is good. What is not good is what we found afterwards. The root cause was a configuration change that somebody had pushed on Friday evening without a review, and nobody had documented it. So the four hours we spent looking for the problem were spent in the wrong place. From now on, two rules. No configuration change ships without a review, and every change gets a contingency. I will send the full report tomorrow.

When I coach people for senior interviews, I always ask the same question first: what had already happened before you arrived? Most candidates skip that part. They start with what they did, and the interviewer has no idea whether the work was hard or easy. If you say I cut downtime to twenty minutes, that means nothing on its own. But if you say the platform had been unstable for a year, the backlog had grown to eight months, and three engineers had left before you took over, then the same sentence is a turnaround. So build every story in two layers. The earlier layer is the situation you inherited. The later layer is what you did about it. English gives you a tense for exactly that, and the candidates who use it well sound like people who understand cause, not just effort.

extra_audio.text: By the time I took over, the team had lost three engineers and the backlog had grown to eight months. The platform had been unstable since 2019, and nobody had ever looked for the root cause. Once we had found the root cause, we rewrote one service and cut downtime to twenty minutes a month. In month three we lost a release, because we had not built a contingency for the migration. By month six the team had regained its momentum and turned the platform around.
